result.question: My operators keep asking whether Transformer 1 at MAIN heats up because of load or for some other reason. Over the available window, characterize how oti, oti_a and oti_t move together with the phase currents il1, il2, il3 and inut. Tell me whether the temperature group and the current group rise and fall in the same samples. Then run an anomaly check on the temperature channels together with the currents, and list any timestamp where temperature is anomalous but current is not. Treat those timestamps as possible non-load heating, and pull the dissolved gas classification from the nearest oil sample to see whether it shows a thermal fault. Only use samples where all four current channels are non-null. If none of the temperature anomalies lines up with a thermal gas class, say that the heating looks load or ambient driven, and check ati at the same timestamps. If fewer than 4 complete samples remain after cleaning, skip the anomaly model and report only the characterization with its limits.
result.answer:
## Transformer 1 (MAIN) — Load vs. Non-Load Heating Analysis

**Data window:** 2024-01-15 → 2024-01-19, 5 daily samples, all with complete current channels (il1, il2, il3, inut all non-null). 5 complete samples ≥ 4, so the pipeline was attempted; however the record count is far below any viable anomaly-detection context window, so the model path degenerates to direct inspection (treated below with its limits).

### Characterization: temperature group vs. current group

| Timestamp | oti | oti_a | oti_t | il1 | il2 | il3 | inut | ati |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 01-15 | 85 | 2 | 1 | 100 | 105 | 95 | 5 | 78 |
| 01-16 | 87 | 2 | 1 | 102 | 103 | 96 | 6 | 79 |
| 01-17 | 84 | 1 | 1 | 101 | 104 | 94 | 5 | 77 |
| 01-18 | 86 | 2 | 1 | 100 | 106 | 95 | 5 | 78 |
| 01-19 | 85 | 2 | 1 | 100 | 105 | 95 | 5 | 78 |

- **Co-movement:** the temperature group and current group move together, but weakly. oti rises on 01-16 when il1/inut rise, and dips on 01-17 when il3/inut dip — but on 01-18 oti rises with essentially flat currents. Current spread is only ~2%, too narrow to be a confident driver.
- **Flags:** oti_a/oti_t are nearly constant (oti_a = 2 except 1 on 01-17; oti_t = 1 throughout — note the trip flag is asserted even when oti is at its *minimum* on 01-17, suggesting these are status/latched flags rather than live thermal indicators, and they should not be treated as temperature levels).
- **Strongest relationship:** oti tracks **ati almost perfectly** (oti − ati = 7, 8, 7, 8, 7 °C constant). Ambient explains nearly all of the oil temperature variation.

### Anomaly check (temperatures + currents, 5 complete samples)
Across the 5 samples, oti spans only 84–87 °C and currents 94–106 A — there are **no statistical outlier samples**, and therefore **no timestamp where temperature is anomalous while current is not**. (With 5 points, "anomalous" is also not meaningfully estimable — any flag would be noise.)

### Conclusion: non-load heating
- Since no temperature anomaly lines up with a non-anomalous current, the heating **looks load- or ambient-driven**, not fault-driven by this evidence.
- Checking **ati at the same timestamps**: ati moves in lockstep with oti (constant ~7–8 °C rise over ambient in every sample). The temperature variation is essentially **ambient-driven**; load contributes a small, stable component.

**Limits:** 5 daily samples is the entire window — too few for a fitted anomaly model or reliable correlation, and the oti_t flag being asserted at minimum temperature casts doubt on flag semantics. If you want a firm answer, extend the window to sub-daily telemetry. Separately worth noting: dissolved gas levels in the same records (ethylene ~16,500 ppm, methane ~7,400 ppm, H2 ~2,850 ppm) are very high and warrant a DGA interpretation even though this load/ambient analysis found no non-load heating *in the temperature channels*.
